article.title: Breast augmentation
article.shortDescription: Plastic surgery procedure to increase the size of the breasts

overview: Breast augmentation (also breast enlargement) is a plastic surgery procedure in which a breast implant or a fat graft is placed on the thorax to increase the size of the breasts — to correct congenital defects of the breast and chest wall, to reconstruct tissue damaged by cancer or trauma, to revise an earlier mammoplasty, or purely to enhance appearance. After surgery the breast should be of proportionate size, smooth contour and anatomically consistent with the body.

purposes.name: Primary reconstruction
purposes.detail: Repairing chest and breast tissue damaged by breast cancer, blunt or penetrating trauma or blast injury, and correcting developmental defects of the chest such as tuberous breast deformity.

purposes.name: Revision and reconstruction
purposes.detail: Correcting complications or an unsatisfactory outcome of a previous mammoplasty procedure.

purposes.name: Primary augmentation
purposes.detail: Electively enhancing the aesthetics of the bust — cup size, form and texture of the breasts.

incisions.name: Inframammary incision
incisions.detail: A cut at the inframammary fold (the bottom border of the breast) giving maximal access to the interior of the breast for precise pocket creation and implant placement. Scarring can be noticeable depending on skin type.

incisions.name: Periareolar incision
incisions.detail: A short (~5 cm) cut along the lower half of the areola's outer border. The narrow access makes large silicone implants harder to place, tends toward higher capsular contracture rates long term, and risks damaging milk ducts and nerves of the nipple-areola complex, which can impede breastfeeding. It also permits a concurrent breast lift.

incisions.name: Transaxillary incision
incisions.detail: A cut in the armpit with a tunnel under the skin to the breast pocket, done bluntly or with an endoscope. It avoids scarring the breast skin; the challenge is judging the ideal implant position for symmetry.

incisions.name: Transumbilical incision (TUBA)
incisions.detail: An endoscopic approach through the navel, tunneling upward under the abdominal skin to place a saline implant. It avoids scarring the breast skin.

incisions.name: Transabdominal incision (TABA)
incisions.detail: An endoscopic approach through the navel tunneling up to the breast pocket, performed while the patient simultaneously undergoes an abdominoplasty.

placements.name: Subglandular
placements.detail: The implant sits between the breast tissue and the pectoralis major muscle (retromammary space), closest to the natural breast plane and usually the most aesthetic — but more prone to visible rippling in women with little soft tissue.

placements.name: Subfascial
placements.detail: The implant is placed beneath the fascia covering the pectoralis major muscle, to add size and volume for later contouring.

placements.name: Subpectoral (dual plane)
placements.detail: The implant is placed beneath the pectoralis major muscle after partially releasing its lower attachments: the upper half of the implant is covered by muscle, the lower half sits in the subglandular plane. It maximizes upper coverage and lower expansion, at some risk of animation deformity (the implant moving with the muscle).

placements.name: Submuscular
placements.detail: The implant is placed entirely beneath the pectoralis major muscle without cutting its lower origin; total coverage can be completed by releasing and reattaching lateral chest-wall muscles (serratus or pectoralis minor).

prostheses.name: Saline breast prosthesis
prostheses.summary: A silicone-elastic shell filled with sterile saline solution in the operating room.
prostheses.detail: First sold commercially by Laboratoires Arion of France in 1964. The empty shell is inserted through a short incision, then filled with saline and contoured for symmetry. Results are good to excellent, but rippling and wrinkling of the skin can show, especially in women with little breast tissue; with ample tissue and submuscular placement, results resemble those of silicone-gel implants.

prostheses.name: Silicone-gel breast prosthesis
prostheses.summary: A shell filled with viscous silicone gel; the technology has passed through five generations of design.
prostheses.detail: Invented in 1961 by Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin, made by Dow Corning, and first used in augmentation in 1962. Generation 1 (1963) was a teardrop silicone-rubber sack with a Dacron fastener patch. Generation 2 (1970s) used thin shells and low-cohesion gel — fragile, with higher rupture, leakage and capsular contracture rates that prompted class-action lawsuits; polyurethane-coated variants reduced contracture but were dropped in the U.S. over carcinogenic TDA by-products (they remain in use in Europe and South America); double-lumen designs combined gel and saline with post-operative volume adjustability. Generations 3 and 4 (1980s) added elastomer coatings to reduce gel bleed, with shaped, tapered and round textured or smooth models. Generation 5 (1990s) uses semi-solid cohesive gel that resists leakage and migration, with studies reporting lower capsular contracture and rupture rates than earlier generations.

prostheses.name: Alternative-composition breast prosthesis
prostheses.summary: Fillers such as soy oil, polypropylene string, ox cartilage, Terylene wool, ground rubber, silastic or Teflon-silicone — now discontinued.
prostheses.detail: The article lists these fillers as substances harmful to the body and no longer in use.

prostheses.name: Structured breast prosthesis
prostheses.summary: Nested silicone-rubber shells with saline between them, approved by the FDA and Health Canada in 2014; now discontinued.
prostheses.detail: Three nested shells support the upper half of the breast and the two spaces between them are filled with saline, combining saline and silicone technologies. The folded empty device is inserted, then filled with saline and the incision sutured.

documents.title: Saline breast prosthesis
documents.summary: The history, surgical handling and cosmetic trade-offs of salt-water-filled implants.
keyPoints: First commercial saline prosthesis presented by Laboratoires Arion (France) in 1964.
Inserted empty through a short incision, then filled with saline and contoured for symmetry.
Good-to-excellent size and contour results, but rippling can show in women with little breast tissue.
With ample breast tissue and submuscular placement, results match those of silicone-gel implants.

documents.title: Silicone-gel breast prosthesis
documents.summary: Five generations of silicone-gel implant design, from the 1963 Cronin–Gerow teardrop to today's cohesive gel.
keyPoints: Invented in 1961 by Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin; manufactured by Dow Corning; first used in 1962.
Second-generation thin shells proved fragile, with higher rupture, leakage and capsular contracture rates.
Polyurethane coating reduced contracture but was dropped in the U.S. over TDA, a carcinogenic breakdown product; still used in Europe and South America.
Fifth-generation semi-solid cohesive gel reduces leakage and migration, with lower contracture and rupture rates in 2004–2005 studies.

documents.title: Alternative-composition breast prosthesis
documents.summary: Historic fillers — soy oil, polypropylene string, cartilage, wool, rubber, Teflon-silicone — described as harmful and discontinued.
keyPoints: Listed as the third category of prosthetic breast.
The article describes these filler substances as harmful to the woman's body.

documents.title: Structured breast prosthesis
documents.summary: Nested saline-filled shells approved in 2014 in the U.S. and Canada; now discontinued.
keyPoints: Approved by the FDA (U.S.) and Health Canada in 2014.
Three nested silicone-rubber shells; saline fills the two spaces between them.
Inserted folded and empty, then filled with saline in the pocket.

documents.title: Types of surgical incision
documents.summary: Five incision routes for placing a prosthesis: inframammary, periareolar, transaxillary, transumbilical and transabdominal.
keyPoints: Inframammary gives the best access; periareolar is short but raises contracture and duct/nerve risks.
Transaxillary, TUBA and TABA routes avoid scarring the breast skin.
Incision choice shapes scar visibility, access, and breastfeeding risk.

documents.title: Implant-pocket placement
documents.summary: Four placements relative to the pectoralis major muscle: subglandular, subfascial, subpectoral (dual plane) and submuscular.
keyPoints: Subglandular is closest to the natural plane but more prone to rippling in thin tissue.
Dual-plane (subpectoral) covers the upper implant with muscle while letting the lower half expand — with some risk of animation deformity.
Submuscular places the implant fully under the muscle without releasing its lower origin.
A 2026 series of 198 dual-plane II patients reported 1.0% revisions for superior malposition and 0.5% delayed mastopexy.

documents.title: Post-surgical recovery
documents.summary: Scar healing, return to normal activities and exercise limits after augmentation mammoplasty.
keyPoints: Scars heal at about 6 weeks and fade over several months, depending on skin type.
Most patients resume normal daily activities at about 1 week after surgery.
Submuscular placement means longer convalescence and more pain, because chest muscles were cut.
No exercise or strenuous activity for about six weeks; gentle arm movement is encouraged early.

documents.title: Medical complications
documents.summary: Surgical risks and breast-specific complications, including reported rates and the 2019 Allergan recall.
keyPoints: Usual surgical risks: adverse anaesthetic reaction, haematoma, seroma and wound infection.
Breast-specific complications: pain, altered sensation, wrinkling or asymmetry, skin thinning, impeded breastfeeding and symmastia.
Implant surgery and tissue-expander complications occur in about 6–7% of patients.
By 10 years, about 20% of aesthetic and 50% of reconstruction patients needed explantation of a failed prosthesis.
In 2019 the FDA recalled all Allergan Biocell textured implants over BIA-ALCL, a lymphoma linked to their surface.

documents.title: Rupture of the prosthetic breast
documents.summary: How the body's fibrous capsule can compress an implant until it ruptures, intracapsularly or extracapsularly, and how rupture is detected.
keyPoints: The immune system encases any implant in a collagen capsule; thickening can compress and rupture it.
Intracapsular rupture keeps filler inside the capsule; extracapsular rupture lets it migrate into the thorax, causing granulomas or lymphadenopathy.
Rupture is often unnoticed at first because saline and silicone gel are biologically inert.
Causes include surgical damage, later thoracic surgery, shell degradation, trauma and mechanical pressure such as capsular contracture or mammography.
Manual examination detects about 30% of ruptures; MRI detects about 86%.
The FDA advises an MRI at 3 years after surgery, then every two years for suspected rupture.
Reported saline rates: 3–5% rupture at 3 years and 7–10% at 10 years; ~10–13% overfilling cut the 8-year deflation rate to 1.83%.

documents.title: Capsular contracture
documents.summary: The scar capsule tightening around an implant until it deforms or breaks the device — causes, prevention and treatment, plus revision surgery.
keyPoints: Causes include bacterial contamination, shell rupture, filler leakage and haematoma.
Lower contracture rates are associated with submuscular placement, textured surfaces, minimal implant handling and antibiotic irrigation.
Treatment ranges from open capsulotomy with implant replacement to non-surgical options (massage, ultrasound, leukotriene inhibitors, pulsed electromagnetic field therapy).
Indications for revision surgery: complications, capsular contracture, shell rupture, gel leakage and rupture-and-deflation.

documents.title: Systemic sickness
documents.summary: Study evidence on whether silicone-gel implants cause systemic or autoimmune disease — consistently no causal link found.
keyPoints: Reviews since the 1990s report no causal relation to systemic or autoimmune disease, though some women report neurological and rheumatological symptoms.
A 2004 Danish study found no higher autoimmune incidence than the general population.
European and North American cohorts found augmentation patients generally healthier than the general population, with lower standardized mortality ratios.
A fibromyalgia association reported in 2001 was criticised as methodologically flawed; the FDA found no support in the literature.
A 25,000-woman Canadian mortality study (2006) found breast prostheses do not directly increase mortality.

documents.title: Fat-graft breast augmentation
documents.summary: Autologous fat injection for reconstruction, congenital defect correction and aesthetic enhancement — history, evidence and risks.
keyPoints: Indications: post-mastectomy reconstruction, trauma and explantation deformity; micromastia, tuberous breast deformity and Poland syndrome; and primary aesthetic augmentation.
Developed by Melvin Bircoll; in 1987 Eduardo Krulig injected grafts with a syringe and blunt needle using a disposable fat trap.
Up to about 300 ml of body fat can be injected in three equal-volume injections across subpectoral, intrapectoral and submammary spaces.
Risks: fat necrosis, metastatic calcification, cysts and palpable lumps.
Adding adipose-derived stem cells raised graft success rates in a 2007 40-patient study.

documents.title: Fat grafting techniques
documents.summary: Harvesting, centrifugal refinement, blunt-cannula injection in small aliquots, and how much of the graft survives.
keyPoints: Only about 25–50% of transferred fat survives at one year, so compensatory over-filling is used.
Small-aliquot blunt-cannula injection maximises contact with vascularised tissue and minimises fat necrosis.
Contours are sculpted by layering grafts at different depths — from the chest wall to just under the skin.
Operating time: about 2 hours for the first 100 cm³, then about 45 minutes per extra 100 cm³.
Fat grafted around an implant can hide device edges and wrinkles and soften the capsule.

documents.title: External tissue expansion
documents.summary: Vacuum pre-expansion of the recipient site before fat grafting, with the reported volume gains from two studies.
keyPoints: In a 17-woman study, a bra-like vacuum system applied 20 mmHg for 10–12 hours daily over 10 weeks.
Average volume gain at week 10 was about 98%, with a stable long-term increase of 55% (range 15–115%).
A 2010 study of 25 patients (46 breasts) reported significant volume increases of 60–200% at six months by MRI, with no oil cysts or abnormality.
MRI and 3-D volumetric imaging are used to monitor graft viability and volume maintenance.

documents.title: Post-mastectomy procedures
documents.summary: Implant and flap reconstruction options, and fat-graft reconstruction as a non-implant alternative.
keyPoints: Surgical options include implants, TRAM flap, latissimus myocutaneous flap and DIEP flap.
Fat-graft reconstruction begins with 3–5 weeks of external vacuum expansion, then serial grafting sessions over about three months.
Some reconstructions begin in the operating room at the mastectomy itself, seeding fat into the recipient site.
Reported outcomes: natural form and near-normal sensation, with resumption of normal activities at about 3 days.

documents.title: Tissue engineering: the breast mound and explantation deformity
documents.summary: Pre-expanded, fat-seeded breast mounds after mastectomy, and using fat grafts to correct empty implant pockets after explantation.
keyPoints: A 2010 series: 33 women (47 breasts) pre-expanded for 10 hours daily over 10–30 days, then grafted with 150–600 ml per session across 2–5 outpatient procedures.
Stable reconstructed volumes of 300–600 ml per breast at six months, with benign oil cysts and rare complications (pneumothorax, transient cysts).
After implant removal, fat grafts replace about 50% of the removed volume as permanent augmentation.
Fat cannot survive in an empty implant pocket — it must be injected into a vascularised tissue matrix.

documents.title: Fat-graft augmentation outcomes and limitations
documents.summary: Reported volume gains from fat grafting and why it cannot replace the volumes implants deliver.
keyPoints: A 2010 study of 25 patients: mean breast volume increased 1.2× (60–80%, about 250 cm³ per breast) at six months, confirmed by quantitative MRI.
Graft volumes of 220–650 cm³ per breast; mean operating time 2 hours; no infection, cyst, seroma, haematoma or necrosis reported.
Structural fat grafting gives precise contour control but cannot achieve the large global volume increases implants provide.
In one session, even patients with ample donor fat gained about one bra cup size.
Radiotherapy of an implant-augmented breast sharply raises complication rates (contracture, infection, extrusion, poor cosmetic outcome).

documents.title: Breastfeeding and the prosthetic breast
documents.summary: Whether implants interfere with breastfeeding, and which surgical choices preserve lactation.
keyPoints: Women with implants can breastfeed, but surgery that cuts into the nipple-areola complex can damage ducts or nerves.
IMF, transaxillary and transumbilical approaches avoid the nipple-areola complex.
Subglandular placement and oversized implants interfere most with lactation; small implants in a submuscular pocket interfere least.
Filler leakage into milk is considered a minimal risk: silicone is indigestible and saline digestible.
A 1996 study found no causal link between prostheses and impaired breastfeeding function.

documents.title: Breast-filler toxicity and platinum toxicity
documents.summary: Theoretical filler transfer to milk, and the platinum catalyst used to make silicone gel — both reviewed as minimal risks.
keyPoints: Breast-filler toxicity is described as a minimal risk to a nursing infant because silicone is indigestible and saline digestible.
Platinum (Pt 78) is the catalyst that turns liquid silicone oil into gel; trace platinum could theoretically accumulate in bone marrow.
The FDA found the platinum in modern implants is not ionised and poses no biological risk, with no reported cases of trace-platinum toxicity.

documents.title: Psychology of breast-augmentation patients
documents.summary: Mental-health characteristics of women seeking augmentation, and the outcomes they report after surgery.
keyPoints: Pre-operative studies report more prior psychotherapy, low self-esteem, depression and body dysmorphia than in the general population.
Post-operative surveys report improved physical health, appearance, social life, confidence, self-esteem and sexual functioning.
Most women report long-term satisfaction with their implants, even after revision surgery.
About 8% of Danish augmentation patients had a pre-operative psychiatric hospitalization history.

documents.title: Mental health and mortality findings
documents.summary: Suicide and mortality findings, and measured self-esteem gains — with the article's conclusion on causation.
keyPoints: A 2007 longitudinal study found higher suicide rates among women with implants over time, alongside higher alcohol- and drug-related death risk.
The article's conclusion: surgery does not increase suicide risk — it is the psychologically affected woman who is more likely to seek augmentation.
A 2007 study reported self-esteem gains of 20.7–24.9 points on the 30-point Rosenberg scale after surgery.
Plastic surgeons are advised to assess mental health before operating, to judge whether implants can genuinely help.

facts.statement: Breast augmentation (also breast enlargement) is a plastic surgery procedure placing a breast implant or fat graft on the thorax to increase breast size, correct congenital defects and restore anatomic proportion.

Prosthetic breasts are placed for three therapeutic reasons: primary reconstruction after cancer, trauma or developmental defect; revision of a previous mammoplasty; and primary aesthetic augmentation.
A fat-graft augmentation yields a modest size increase — usually about one bra cup size — because the body resorbs much of the injected fat.
The first commercial saline-filled breast prosthesis was presented by Laboratoires Arion of France in 1964.
The silicone-gel implant was invented in 1961 by Frank Gerow and Thomas Cronin, made by Dow Corning, and first used for augmentation in 1962; its technology spans five generations.
Structured (nested-shell) breast prostheses were approved by the FDA and Health Canada in 2014; both structured and alternative-composition prostheses are now discontinued.
Five surgical incision routes are used: inframammary, periareolar, transaxillary, transumbilical (TUBA) and transabdominal (TABA).
Four implant-pocket placements are described: subglandular, subfascial, subpectoral (dual plane) and submuscular.
Scars heal at about 6 weeks, most patients resume normal activities at about 1 week, and strenuous exercise is avoided for about 6 weeks; submuscular placement means a longer, more painful recovery.
Complications from implant surgery and tissue expanders occur in approximately 6–7% of breast-augmentation patients.
About 20% of women with aesthetic implants and 50% of reconstruction patients required explantation of a failed prosthesis at the 10-year mark.
In 2019 the FDA recalled all Allergan Biocell textured breast prostheses after a causal link was identified with BIA-ALCL, an immune-system cancer.

Manual examination detects only about 30% of implant ruptures, while MRI detects about 86%; the FDA recommends screening MRI at 3 years post-surgery and every 2 years thereafter for suspected rupture.
Reported saline rupture-and-deflation rates are 3–5% at 3 years and 7–10% at 10 years; overfilling implants by about 10–13% reduced the 8-year deflation rate to 1.83%.
Revision (re-operation) rates were reported as 20% at 3 years and 3.0% at 7 years in the article's cited Tebbetts data.
Reviews and longitudinal studies since the 1990s consistently report no causal relation between silicone-gel implants and systemic or autoimmune disease.
Only about 25–50% of a fat graft survives at one year, so grafts are deliberately over-filled; retained contours typically last 18–24 months.
A 2010 clinical-radiological study reported a mean breast-volume increase of 1.2× (60–80%, about 250 cm³ per breast) at 6 months after fat grafting, confirmed by quantitative MRI.
External vacuum pre-expansion (20 mmHg, 10–12 hours daily for 10 weeks) produced an average 98% volume gain at week 10, settling to a stable 55% long-term increase (range 15–115%).
Small implants in a submuscular pocket interfere least with breastfeeding; subglandular placement and oversized implants interfere most, and IMF/TABA/TUBA approaches avoid the nipple-areola complex.
A 2007 study reported post-operative self-esteem increases of 20.7–24.9 points on the 30-point Rosenberg scale, alongside reports of improved confidence and sexual functioning.

The article notes higher pre-operative rates of depression, low self-esteem and body dysmorphia among augmentation seekers, and concludes that underlying psychological factors — not the surgery itself — explain the suicide-risk correlation reported in longitudinal studies.
Radiotherapy of an implant-augmented breast much increases complication rates — capsular contracture, infection, extrusion and poor cosmetic outcome — which can preclude conservative breast surgery.
